tagline: A desert lakeshore road beside the largest remnant of Lake Lahontan
intro: Pyramid Lake Road follows the lake’s western shore through Sutcliffe to Warrior Point Park Road, north of town. On the approach from Sparks, SR 445 narrows to two lanes in Palamino Valley before entering the Pyramid Lake Indian Reservation. The Federal Highway Administration lists the broader Pyramid Lake National Scenic Byway at 30.2 miles, allowing two hours including backtracking, and highlights its desert lake and migrating waterfowl. The Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe describes the water changing between blue and gray with the sky above. The Tribe identifies the lake as the largest remnant of ancient Lake Lahontan and asks visitors to respect the lake and land as sacred.

SR 445 was assembled from older routes during Nevada’s late-1970s highway renumbering. The first two miles in Sparks had been SR 32; most of the remaining road came from SR 33. The 12.5 miles inside the reservation received state scenic-byway designation on June 27, 1996, followed by national designation on July 15.

Travel south from the SR 445 terminus at Warrior Point Park Road through Sutcliffe along the west shore. At the SR 446 junction, that road connects to Nixon, home to the Tribe’s museum and visitor center. The broader designated corridor includes parts of SR 446 and SR 447 as well as SR 445.

moments.title: The Pyramid
moments.text: The Pyramid is a small island near the lake’s southeastern shore, also called Fremont’s Pyramid or Pyramid Island. The formation lies slightly less than six miles from Sutcliffe and approximately 1.2 miles northeast of Anaho Island. John C. Frémont gave the lake its English name after its pyramid-shaped tufa formations. A white calcium-carbonate band east of the island records a time when the lake stood at or near its overflow point. The Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe considers the lake and land sacred and lists the Pyramid/Stone Mother area as closed to the public.

moments.title: Anaho Island
moments.text: Anaho Island protects a colony of American white pelicans within a national wildlife refuge covering the entire island. This rocky island is a little more than a mile long in both directions at its widest dimensions. It lies approximately four miles east of Sutcliffe, in the southeastern part of the lake. Its breeding birds also include California gulls, Caspian terns and double-crested cormorants. Anaho is the lake’s largest tufa formation, and its access restrictions protect the island’s ecology. The Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe lists the island as closed to the public.

moments.title: Sutcliffe
moments.text: Sutcliffe stands on Pyramid Lake’s western bank, beside the largest remaining part of ancient Lake Lahontan. The Truckee River supplies the lake, mostly with water flowing out of Lake Tahoe. There is no surface outlet: water leaves through evaporation or underground seepage. The Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe identifies this lake as the world’s only habitat for the Cui-ui fish. In Sutcliffe, the Tribe’s ranger station sells permits for visits to the lake. The Tribe’s museum in Nixon includes exhibits on the Cui-ui and Lahontan cutthroat trout, alongside displays on tribal culture and history.

practical: The Pyramid: The Pyramid/Stone Mother area is closed to the public. (checked 2026-10-11)
Anaho Island: Anaho Island is closed to the public. (checked 2026-10-11)
Sutcliffe: Swimming or camping requires a valid tribal permit, available online or at the ranger station in Sutcliffe. (checked 2026-10-11)
